newsitem.title: UK: Ministers urge calm as cloning fears spread.
newsitem.headline: Ministers urge calm as cloning fears spread.

text.p: Government ministers across Europe tried to settle qualms about cloning on Thursday, promising thorough checks on scientists and bans on carbon-copy humans, after news that a sheep had been cloned.
But newspapers invoked images of "master races" and movie stars on production lines, while politicians demanded speedy investigations of just what genetic researchers are doing.

Ian Wilmut and colleagues at Scotland's Roslin Institute and biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics Pls caused a global uproar when they announced they had cloned a sheep -- the first time an adult animal had been successfully cloned.

European Commission President Jacques Santer joined the furore by asking an EU biotechnology advisory team of scientists, lawyers and ethicists to investigate whether the European Union should take a stance on cloning.
Britain was one step ahead, with its Human Genetic Advisory Commission, put together last year to examine such issues, meeting for the first time on Thursday.
Sir Colin Campbell, a legal philosopher and chairman of the new committee, said it was certain to discuss cloning. "It would be perverse of us not to talk about it," he told BBC radio.
British Science Minister Ian Taylor said Campbell's committee and others would keep a close eye on scientists.

"For those who fear that science fiction will come true, they should be clear that a broad range of regulatory controls have been put in place to prevent what is undesirable becoming a reality," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has ordered the U.S. National Bioethics Advisory Panel to report within 90 days on the legal and ethical ramifications of cloning.

But National Institutes of Health Director Dr Harold Varmus said he was worried about "the rush to legislation". "We have a new discovery," he told the House Appropriations subcommittee that controls NIH spending. "It needs to be absorbed and discussed."

Guy Paillotin, president of the National Institute for Agricultural Research (INRA), a state-funded research agency, said real scientific issues were being sidetracked by talk of mad scientists cloning humans. "We must say very loudly that this is out of the question, that this is stupid," he said.
But Axel Kahn, director of the INSERM genetics laboratory at the Cochin Institute in Paris, said people may demand just that.

"Today's society is characterised by an increasing demand for biological inheritance, as if this were the only form of inheritance worthy of the name," he wrote in a commentary for the Nature science journal.

Kahn noted that sterile or infertile people had flocked to take advantage of new in-vitro fertilisation (IVF or test-tube) techniques. Lesbians could now possibly demand the right to genetic progeny without the input of a man, he argued.
German newspapers raised the spectre of Nazi eugenics experiments, when scientists tried to create an Aryan blond-haired and blue-eyed "master race".

"The cloning of human beings would fit precisely into Adolf Hitler's world view," wrote Die Welt newspaper, in a comment that recalled the film "The Boys from Brazil". "And there is no doubt that he would have used this technology intensively if it were available at that time."
Die Welt worried that, even if nations promised not to clone humans, there was no guarantee that strong personalities with big egos and enough wealth could clone themselves surreptitiously.

"With the cloning of an adult creature, humans can put an end to evolution," said the business daily Handelsblatt. "We have crossed a barrier we should have left standing. The birth of the sheep Dolly is an event not unlike the first nuclear explosion."

The liberal weekly newspaper Die Zeit noted that it might some day be possible for women to reproduce without any contribution from men. "How long will it take now until a new Einstein, Lollobrigida or even Hitler populates the brave new world?" it asked.

There was some humour. Munich's Abendzeitung printed five identical pictures of a smiling Chancellor Helmut Kohl over a front-page banner headline that read: "Genetic researchers say they could now clone Kohl."
